REVIEWER #2:
2.1 The authors use a dimensionality reduction technique to evaluate the contribution of brain geometry
and connectivity to regional dynamics. While the paper is well written and the analysis is performed
carefully, I have many concerns about the approach to integrate data across subjects that leave me less
enthusiastic of the interpretation of the findings.
We thank the Reviewer for their positive feedback on the writing and analytical precision of the paper. We
address their concerns on the group-level nature of our approach in the points below.
2.2 I fully understand the difficulties of working with iEEG data that is clinically acquired. In each
patient, electrodes will be placed for clinical reasons, and it is therefore difficult if not impossible to
achieve similar coverage of brain activity recordings across patients – each patient will have recordings from different brain areas. In order to achieve full coverage of brain areas, here the authors employ a
technique of mapping the data from all patients onto a single common space. While they are not the first
to use this approach, I am not convinced that it is appropriate for the types of questions that the authors
want to answer about the data. By looking at group level data, the authors are fundamentally choosing
to ignore individual differences across the population that I believe would be essential to preserve in
order to truly ask about questions of how brain geometry, connectivity, and dynamics are related. We
know that both structural and functional brain connectivity can be used to perform fingerprinting of
individuals. I have the following very specific concerns about how individual variability is ignored in
this data.
Assessing interindividual consistency of iEEG-MRI associations was beyond the scope of the present paper,
which rather aimed to uncover fundamental principles of brain organization expressed across individuals.
We emphasize the leaps enabled by group-level iEEG studies in functional human brain mapping, making
it a well-suited technique for our objective (discussed in response to point 2.6). Importantly, we developed
two supplementary analyses that directly assess the question of individual-level replicability of our findings.
These analyses and corresponding supplementary figures (FIGURE S11 and FIGURE S12) are described in
detail in our responses to point 2.7 and 2.8. In summary, these supplementary analyses show that (1) the
proximity of nodes in the embedding space captures the similarity of channel PSDs in held-out patients,
and (2) the relative differences in modality-specific iEEG-MRI correlations generalize to the single-patient
level (i.e., strongest associations with GD, followed by SC, and similar associations to FC and MPC).
For completeness, we more clearly acknowledge the limitations of our approach in the revised DISCUSSION.
Intracranial EEG indeed presents challenges for interindividual comparisons compared to techniques with
consistent brain coverage. However, it is a powerful technique both in its unique spatiotemporal precision
and in its ability to directly record neural activity. We thus balance discussions of technical limitations by
highlighting how such approaches can still bring valuable insights into our fundamental understanding of
brain organization (p.15):
“Nonetheless, investigations of human brain organization using iEEG are limited by the technique’s unique challenges,
including its restricted accessibility, exclusive use in clinical settings, as well as sparse and patient-specific sampling
(111). It also remains an open question to what extent focal epileptic activity in one brain region might affect activity
in the rest the brain and skew the generalizability of iEEG findings to healthy brain function. Recent data sharing
initiatives, such as the resource used here (18) and others (8, 112-115), have been instrumental in addressing these
limitations. Although iEEG data is collected in a clinical context, pooling carefully curated single-patient data
significantly boosts spatial coverage, thus enabling novel explorations of brain cartography and facilitating the
identification of overarching principles of neural organization. These innovations add on to the recognized advantages
of iEEG regarding its high spatiotemporal precision to study human brain function, as well as its specificity to neural
signals over methods offering full brain coverage such as fMRI (113). Studies focusing on group-level inference, such
as the present work, thus offer new perspectives for human brain mapping to which other modalities may be blind.
Group-level paradigms are a valuable first step towards more targeted individual-level inquiries able to clarify
populational variations. For example, by testing the consistency of these principles across individuals, extreme
deviations from the population norm can be identified and related to clinical presentations (3).”
2.3 In the Discovery Cohort, not only are all subjects mapped onto a single common space, but also, the
left hemisphere is flipped to be on the right hemisphere and only one side of the brain is considered. This
adds further distortion to the data as it assumes perfect symmetry between both left and right dynamics
and connectivity, on top of ignoring individual differences between subjects. Although there is some
mention of using patient specific data in the Replication Cohort, from what I can tell, for the iEEG data,
ultimately this same group level mapping was performed.
While we expand our discussion of group-level analyses in response to other points, we indeed mapped all
channels to a single hemisphere to further improve spatial coverage of the cortex. Nonetheless, control
analyses in FIGURE S4 demonstrate that highly similar gradients are obtained when preserving the bilateral
distribution of channels (i.e., when no flipping was applied). These findings are also reported in the main
manuscript (p.6), suggesting that gradient findings were not significantly affected by this decision to map
channels to a single hemisphere:
“We also replicated our findings when preserving the bilateral distribution of channels and applying a lower
resolution parcellation (Schaefer-100) to maintain broad cortical coverage (FIGURE S4). The high correspondence of
G1 (vertexwise Spearman correlation r =0.767; r =0.804) and G2 (vertexwise Spearman correlation r =0.645;
left right left
r =0.671) topographies with gradients derived from our main analysis provides additional support for the
right
independence of our findings to parcellation choice.”
We also edited the DISCUSSION to encourage explorations of asymmetries in iEEG signals across
hemispheres in future work (p.15):
“Future studies based on even larger datasets or providing a high proportion of bilaterally implanted cases may
furthermore help to elucidate principles of asymmetry in neural dynamic across the two hemispheres.”
2.4 Structural connectivity analysis was also performed at the group level, and additionally, the
connection weights in the group level matrix were log-transformed to reduce variance in connectivity
strength. However, presumably, the differences in connectivity strength are important! Again, these are
related to individual differences. Functional connectivity for rsfMRI data was also group averaged,
ignoring patient-specific differences.
Regarding structural connectivity (SC), we followed established procedures for group-level analyses of this
modality as described in previous work (Betzel et al., 2019a). Specifically, distance-dependent consensus
thresholding leverages edge length data to preserve topological parameters of subject-level networks by
reliably representing both short- and long-range connections at the group-level. Resulting SC weights are
however highly skewed, with few very strong connections and many weak or zero connections (as is also
the case at the individual-level). This property of SC matrix weights violates assumptions of normality but
can notably be mitigated by log-transforming edge values (Hansen et al., 2023; Sebenius et al., 2023; van
den Heuvel et al., 2015). Given that statistical methods used here assume normality of the underlying data
(i.e., Pearson correlation, multilinear regression), this log-transformation is an adequate transformation to
optimize analytical validity (Nelson et al., 2023). We have added this explanation to the revised manuscript
(p.19):
“Group-level structural connectivity (SC) was computed using distance-dependent thresholding to preserve the
distribution of within- and between-hemisphere connection lengths found in individual subjects (140). However, SC
weights of the resulting matrix remain highly skewed, with few very strong connections and many weak or zero
connections. As this property of the matrix violates assumptions of normality, which is problematic for the statistical
tests applied in the present work, connection weights in the resulting group-level were log-transformed to reduce
connectivity strength variance.”
We agree with the Reviewer that individual differences in SC, FC, and other modalities leveraged in our
work are important topics of investigation. However, we respectfully disagree that individual-focused
approaches should necessarily be conducted at the expense of discovering general principles of brain
organization expressed at the group-level. While we argue in favour of the importance and relevance of
group-level inference throughout this response (notably in points 2.6, 2.7, and 2.8), several steps in our
processing pipeline were taken to sample individual-specific data as precisely as possible using state-of
the-art techniques. For example, surface-based features such as the timeseries used to generate the FC
matrices and the intensity profiles used to generate MPC matrices are sampled in the participant’s native
space for each modality, limiting data interpolation with co-registration to a standard space. Geodesic
distance measurements also relied on high-resolution, native space surfaces. These procedures are
implemented in addition to the SC consensus thresholding approach described above. This information is
now more clearly highlighted in the revised manuscript (p.18):
“Imaging data were processed with micapipe (v0.2.3; micapipe.readthedocs.io/), an openly available pipeline for
multimodal MRI processing, data fusion, and multiscale connectome generation (119). This pipeline is notably
adapted to sample features in modality-specific spaces, therefore limiting data blurring that can occur with co-
registration to a standard template space.”
2.5 At the microscale, it seems that patient-specific matrices were obtained. I don’t understand how this
analysis can be considered comparable to the others that were performed at the group level.
We believe the Reviewer is referring to the microstructural profile covariance (MPC) matrices, which were
computed at the patient-level and subsequently parcellated and averaged across individuals for all analyses
involving the iEEG data. This is the case for all MRI-derived modalities, which we clarify in the revised
manuscript (p.6):
“Matrices were computed for each participant and averaged across individuals (for details on data processing,
analysis, and group-level aggregation, see MATERIALS AND METHODS).”
2.6 The data used in this study all comes from patients with epilepsy. As each patient has a different focus
of their seizures and potential lesions in different locations, even when the channels are selected from
“healthy” regions, it is to be expected that the underlying brain connectivity and resulting dynamics are
affected. This should lead to increased individual variability within each cohort, making it even less
reasonable to perform a group level analysis.
The Reviewer is correct that patients referred for iEEG often show a complex clinical presentation (e.g.,
inconclusive or contradictory localization findings using non-invasive methods). This may increase some
degrees of variation across participants due to different seizure loci locations and clinical etiologies.
However, the stringent data selection procedure of the MNI Open iEEG Atlas and Replication cohort
removing channels involved in epileptogenic processes (i.e., excluding channels located in abnormal tissue;
selection of segments days after implantation; selection of segments several hours away from a seizure; no
segments selected after stimulation; absence of interictal discharges or slow-wave anomalies; consistent
recording conditions) helps mitigate these concerns. Furthermore, the replication analyses presented in our
paper indicate good generalizability of our findings across two distinct cohorts, despite variability in clinical
presentations in these samples.
We respectfully disagree with the Reviewer that this limitation of iEEG studies pertaining to inter-patient
variability make group-level analysis inappropriate for the objective of our study, that is the discovery of
general principles of brain organization. Historically, iEEG recordings performed in patients with epilepsy
have led to significant contributions to our understanding and mapping of brain function. For example,
intracranial stimulation studies have produced representative maps of the cortical organization of function,
namely the motor and sensory homunculi (Penfield & Boldrey, 1937), and there have been further exciting
developments in our understanding of brain network organization based on recent applications of
stimulation techniques (Momi et al., 2025). Aggregation of functional connectivity maps in predefined
frequency bands across patients implanted with ECoG can replicate network topographies found using rs-
fMRI in healthy cohorts (Betzel et al., 2019b). Similarly, iEEG recordings allow the measurement of neural
timescales from power spectrum density characteristics (Gao et al., 2020; Honey et al., 2012), with longer
timescales in association cortex relative to sensory and motor regions replicating fMRI findings in healthy
individuals (Golesorkhi et al., 2021). Moreover, recordings in putatively normal tissue are increasingly used
to build normative maps of cortical dynamics and can accurately identify abnormal brain dynamics in
unseen data on a region-specific basis (Bernabei et al., 2022; Taylor et al., 2022). This suggest that datasets
such as the MNI Open iEEG Atlas provide a valid normative repertoire of inter-individual variability in
cortical dynamics amenable to investigations of group-level characteristics of these maps. Patients with
different epileptogenic zone locations can also undergo the same task to clarify the topography and
dynamics associated with different experimental conditions. For example, signals originating from deep
structures such as the insula (Das & Menon, 2024; Huang et al., 2025), medial temporal lobe (Solomon et
al., 2019), and amygdala (Wang et al., 2017) can be precisely captured with invasive techniques such as
iEEG. For significant group-level effects to be detected, individual-level effects must present a reasonable
level of consistency, despite the clinical heterogeneity of the study sample. Similarly, many features of
general brain organization can be replicated in patients: in epilepsy, we can find similar sets of canonical
network communities and macroscale gradient patterns (Cabalo et al., 2024; Maneshi et al., 2014; Royer et
al., 2023; Xie et al., 2024), and the spread of abnormal dynamics can be accurately modelled using
connectome information derived from healthy samples (Xia et al., 2025) . While quantitative differences
have been observed in patients vs. controls on metrics derived from these modalities (e.g., connectivity
strength, balance of segregation/integration of networks (Coito et al., 2016; Larivière et al., 2020a)), the
preservation of these global principles supports the utility of patient studies to improve our understanding
of human brain dynamics despite the presence of patient-specific disease-related alterations.
Nonetheless, even with careful selection of data segments, it remains an open question to what extent focal
epileptic activity in one brain region might affect activity in the rest the brain. We now acknowledge this in
the revised DISCUSSION (p.15), in the segment cited in point 2.2.
2.7 I assume that the reason that the analysis was performed on two cohorts was to alleviate some of
these concerns about group level analysis. However, I still believe that while the “average” analysis
might be similar in 2 cohorts, the actual findings could simply not hold in either. In any sort of population
that has sub-groups within the population or even just simply lots of variability across the population,
one can detect relationships between the average geometry and structure with average dynamics that
simply do not exist for any of the individuals in the population.
The Reviewer is correct that the analysis performed in the Replication cohort (Figure 4) served to assess
the robustness of findings reported in the main cohort to a distinct sample of participants. We now report
this clearly in the RESULTS (p.11):
“We lastly leveraged an independent patient cohort to assess the replicability of macroscale gradients of neural
dynamics and their association with within-sample neuroimaging metrics.”
While group-level findings can be difficult to generalize to individual-level inference, the objective of the
present work was rather to identify general principles of brain organization from neurophysiological data
and their network-level correlates. For example, the sensory-association axis is known to be repeatedly
expressed across structural, functional, and molecular modalities (Sydnor et al., 2021), yet its exact
topography varies throughout development and aging (Bethlehem et al., 2020; Larivière et al., 2020b), as
well as across disease states (Hong et al., 2019). We do not deny that there is likely inter-individual
heterogeneity in the expression of these principles and their relationships across modalities, and that aspects
of these dimensions and their coupling likely relate to symptoms and behaviour (Baum et al., 2020; Paquola
et al., 2019; Royer et al., 2023). These questions, however, are beyond the scope of the present study.
Nonetheless, our work represents a first step in identifying these overarching dimensions of brain
organization and sets the foundation for future work implementing these techniques at an individual level.
To address the Reviewer’s concerns regarding individual-level replicability, we designed two additional
analyses (see also point 2.8). We first sought to assess if the group-level embedding space could capture
individual-level similarity in PSD architectures. To do so, we regenerated the group-level gradient space
while iteratively excluding each subject, and calculated embedding distances in each group-level space. For
the left-out subject at each iteration, we evaluated if the proximity of sampled nodes in the embedding space
was related to the similarity of corresponding channel PSDs covered by the gradient parcels. PSD similarity
was assessed using a partial correlation of channel PSDs, while controlling for the within-subject average.
We specifically compared partial correlation values at short embedding distances (embedding distance <20th
percentile) versus long embedding distances (embedding distance >80th percentile) for each patient. In all
patients, channel PSDs were more highly correlated across nodes situated closer in the embedding space
computed from the remaining 17 patients, although the strength of this effect varied across individuals
(FIGURE S12).
We report this analysis in the revised RESULTS (p.11-12) and include this additional figure below:
“Furthermore, reconstructing the embedding space while iteratively excluding each patient found that embedding
distances between nodes related to channel-specific PSD similarity in the held-out patient (FIGURE S12).”
gradient space was regenerated while iteratively excluding each subject, and we calculated embedding
distances in each group-level space. For the left-out subject at each iteration, we evaluated if the proximity
of sampled nodes in the embedding space was related to the similarity of corresponding channel PSDs
covered by the gradient parcels. PSD similarity was assessed using a partial correlation of channel PSDs,
while controlling for the within-subject average. We specifically compared partial correlation values at
short embedding distances (embedding distance <20th percentile) versus long embedding distances
(embedding distance >80th percentile) for each patient. In all patients (each represented by their own
boxplot), PSDs were more highly correlated across nodes situated closer in the embedding space computed
from the remaining 17 patients, although the strength of this effect varied across individuals (mean T-
statistic=16.004; S.D.=13.152). All p-values are FDR-corrected.
2.8 While I understand the desire to fully cover the brain with the iEEG data, I think that to do this study
properly, one would have to perform the gradient analysis separately for each individual, and accept that
between individuals, the spatial coverage would be different. I realize that this makes it hard to collapse
the analysis across individuals and perform regional analysis, but at least one could look at the
correlations between gradients and structure at the individual level and later try to find where there was
spatial overlap between patients to do a limited spatial analysis.
The Reviewer’s point is well taken that individual-level investigations would strengthen presented group-
level findings. For this reason, we provide a new supplementary analysis and figure in which gradients of
neural dynamics were generated for each patient independently, over covered regions. To improve coverage,
we also mapped all contacts to a single hemisphere as in our group analysis (although only 4/18 patients
had bilateral implantations). We computed embedding distance matrices for each patient and calculated
edgewise correlations with MRI measures derived from each patient’s own data. The distribution of
correlation coefficients is presented in FIGURE S11:
Figure S11. Individual-level correspondence of iEEG-MRI associations in Replication cohort. We
computed patient-specific gradients from covered regions and computed the embedding distance between
available nodes for gradients explaining up to 50% in the input data. Bilateral implantations were mapped
to the right hemisphere (n=4), left-sided implantations were flipped to the right hemisphere (n=5), and
right hemisphere implantation were analysed without flipping (n=9). For each patient, embedding
distances were correlated with MRI features of corresponding nodes, and resulting correlation coefficients
(Pearson r) are represented as black markers. Each black dot represents a single patient, with the group
distribution shown in ridge plots for each modality (black line: median). Replicating group-level findings
in the Discovery cohort, similarity of neural dynamics in the cortex were most strongly correlated with
geodesic distance (GD; median r=-0.325), followed by structural connectivity (SC; median r = -0.249),
and lower associations with functional connectivity (median r = -0.151) and microstructural profile
covariance (median r = -0.156).
These findings are also reported in the revised RESULTS (p.11) and DISCUSSION (p.14-15):
“Additional replication analyses implemented at the individual level also found stronger associations with GD relative
to other modalities, followed by SC and balanced correlations with FC and MPC (FIGURE S11).”
“Indeed, translating our approach at an individual-level revealed considerable inter-individual variability in the
magnitude of multimodal association. However, given the technical limitations of iEEG, it is difficult to disentangle
the relative contributions of individual differences in brain organization versus spatial sampling effects in explaining
this variability.”
15
2.9 In summary, because this work is based on group averaged data, making it hard to know where true
correlations might exist at the individual level, I do not feel that it has the ability to be of high impact to
the field.
We are confident that our answers and new individual-level analyses in the Replication cohort (point 2.8)
have helped address the Reviewer’s concerns. We agree with the Reviewer that there is certainly high value
in identifying sources of individual uniqueness. However, and as outlined in our response, numerous
important findings in neuroscience focus on group-average data to identify general principles of human
brain organization, an endeavour to which to which we contribute through the present work.
2.10 (Remarks on code availability): Because I have issues with the fundamental assumptions about the
data set, I did not review any code.
The code remains openly available for independent review.
REVIEWER #3:
Signed Review (Stuart Oldham)
3.1 In this work, Royer et al. investigate how regional dynamics, as measured by iEEG, are constrained
by geometric, microstructural, and connectomic features. They find that geodesic distances strongly
constrain brain dynamics, but this relationship is weakest in transmodal cortices, consistent with other
findings showing that neuronal organisation in these regions clearly departs from that in the rest of the
brain. The authors further strengthen the reliability of their findings by using a replication dataset,
where they observe similar results. This is a very well-written paper, with excellent figures and good
science! 😊 I have no major concerns, and my comments are largely restricted to suggestions on how the
authors could improve the manuscript and enhance clarity where needed.
We thank Dr. Oldham for the positive assessment and thoughtful suggestions to improve our paper.
3.2 As the authors will be oh so very well aware, there are many papers now correlating gradients with
all the other gradients and all the other brain related things, so it is easy to get lost in what has been done
before and where something clearly novel is actually being done. To the best of my knowledge, this is the
first study using iEEG, correct? If so, I think this is worth highlighting more explicitly as a key novelty.
I suggest making it very clear in the Introduction how this technique provides insights that previous
methods could not. At present, the importance of using iEEG is somewhat underemphasised.
To our knowledge, our paper is indeed the first to derive gradients from iEEG data. In accordance with the
Reviewer’s suggestion, we now further emphasize the novelty of our approach in INTRODUCTION (p.3-4):
“The present work established a novel approach to fill this gap by uncovering large-scale gradients of neural dynamics
and relating this complex activity landscape to underlying multiscale anatomy.”
“These gradients, mapped for the first time in iEEG data in the present work, captured the coordinate system of neural
rhythms in the neocortex, grouping regions with similar neurophysiology independently of their anatomical location.”
3.3 All iEEG data used in this study were obtained from patients. Given that these individuals have
epilepsy, and would be expected to exhibit altered patterns of brain activity, how applicable are the
findings to non-clinical populations? Or is it assumed that, outside of seizure episodes, patients’ brain
activity patterns are comparable to those of non-epileptic individuals?
While iEEG presents unique advantages in terms of spatiotemporal precision, data collection with this
technique is indeed limited to clinical populations, and particularly people with epilepsy. Without direct
access to equivalent data in healthy populations, it is difficult to ascertain how generalizable the present
findings are to non-clinical cohorts. However, different sets of findings allow us to speculate that results
may at least partially replicate in healthy samples. First, using resources such as the MNI Open iEEG atlas
(as in the present work) as a normative dataset, previous studies could accurately identify abnormal brain
dynamics in unseen data (Bernabei et al., 2022; Taylor et al., 2022). This suggests relatively homogeneous
regional properties at the group-level, perhaps reflecting typical neurophysiological processes allowing the
detection of regional divergence from a normative distribution of neural dynamics. Second, previous work
applying dimensionality reduction to a large number of timeseries features derived from
magnetoencephalography data collected in healthy participants showed a principal component notably
separating unimodal and transmodal cortical systems (Shafiei et al., 2023), similar to the present study.
We revised the DISCUSSION to include this information (p.15):
“Nonetheless, investigations of human brain organization using iEEG are limited by the technique’s unique challenges,
including its restricted accessibility, exclusive use in clinical settings, as well as sparse and patient-specific sampling
(113). It also remains an open question to what extent focal epileptic activity in one brain region might affect activity
in the rest the brain and skew the generalizability of iEEG findings to healthy brain function. Recent data sharing
initiatives, such as the resource used here (18) and others (8, 114-117), have been instrumental in addressing these
limitations. Although iEEG data is collected in a clinical context, pooling carefully curated single-patient data
significantly boosts spatial coverage, thus enabling novel explorations of brain cartography and facilitating the
identification of overarching principles of neural organization. These innovations add on to the recognized advantages
of iEEG regarding its high spatiotemporal precision to study human brain function, as well as its specificity to neural
signals over methods offering full brain coverage such as fMRI (113). Studies focusing on group-level inference, such
as the present work, thus offer new perspectives for human brain mapping to which other modalities may be blind.
Group-level paradigms are a valuable first step towards more targeted individual-level inquiries able to clarify
populational variations. For example, by testing the consistency of these principles across individuals, extreme
deviations from the population norm can be identified and related to clinical presentations (3). Future studies based
on even larger datasets or providing a high proportion of bilaterally implanted cases may furthermore help to
elucidate principles of asymmetry in neural dynamic across the two hemispheres.”
3.4 In the main analysis using the Discovery Cohort, iEEG data from patients were combined with
SC/FC/MPC measures calculated in healthy individuals. However, for the replication cohort, were both
the iEEG and MRI-derived measures calculated in the same patient cohort (i.e., was SC/FC/MPC
calculated for the MNI clinical cohort and used in the analysis)? I believe this is what was done, but if
so, could it be made more explicit? More broadly, the main concern here is that data from healthy and
clinical populations are being combined and used to make general inferences about brain organisation.
This issue is briefly acknowledged on lines 445–446 (“as well as epilepsy-related changes in SC that
could only be detected in a within-patient design”), but I think a clearer discussion or acknowledgement
of this limitation should be made.
The main analyses performed in the Discovery cohort indeed focus on cross-dataset comparisons, while the
Replication cohort uses within-sample data. As requested, we clarified this in the revised RESULTS (p.4):
“For the main analyses, we leveraged a Discovery cohort (MNI open iEEG atlas, n=106) in which iEEG data were
aggregated in stereotaxic space (18). We assessed correspondence to neural organization derived from two high-
definition MRI datasets acquired in 50 healthy individuals at 3T and 10 healthy individuals at 7T. Our main analyses
thus rest on a design comparing iEEG and imaging modalities across different datasets. We then evaluate the
generalizability of our findings using a fully independent Replication cohort (MNI clinical dataset, n=18), where both
iEEG and multimodal pre-surgical MRI data were available in each participant for within-cohort comparison of
modalities.”
We also expanded our DISCUSSION to acknowledge potential limitations of this approach (p.14):
“Cross-referencing iEEG data collected in patients with MRI measures acquired in healthy participants allowed us
to maximize spatial coverage and sample sizes in our Discovery cohort analyses. This approach is in line with the
widespread use of data contextualization techniques in neuroscience, which measures and integrates distinct maps of
human brain organization (107). However, this remains a limitation of the present work, as it is unclear to what extent
findings from these distinct cohorts generalize to overall principles of brain organization.”
3.5 All analyses are conducted in a single hemisphere (due to understandable technical constraints).
Especially when we consider that the pattern of inter-hemispheric connections is very different to intra-
hemispheric connections and virtually all such inter-hemispheric connections are long-range, which as
the authors note seem to have some special role in shaping communication across brain networks (thus
inter-hemispheric dynamics might be very different!). At a minimum, would be worth noting as a
limitation.
We explore this suggestion by using data mapped to the Schaefer-100 parcellation. We use this parcellation
in our supplementary analysis assessing the replicability of our findings in a lower resolution parcellation
preserving the bilateral distribution of channels in the MNI Open iEEG atlas (FIGURE S4). When computing
the embedding distances on this bilaterally mapped data and correlating edge values with corresponding
SC, FC, and MPC entries, we find a similar sequence of correlation strengths across modalities: SC r=-
0.322; FC r=-0.217; MPC r=-0.185 (as in the main analyses where SC |r| > FC |r| > MPC |r|). As GD is only
computed within hemisphere, we could not include it in this analysis.
We report these findings in the revised RESULTS (p.7):
“Findings were replicable […] when computing correlations between embedding distances and MRI measures from
bilaterally mapped data (SC r = -0.322; FC r = -0.217; MPC r = -0.185).”
3.6. I found it interesting that the first two gradients explain relatively little variance, whereas most other
decompositions of brain features based on regional similarity or covariance explain much more. Do the
authors have any intuition as to why this might be?
The variance explained by the different gradients is indeed quite balanced here. This observation notably
guided our choice of using all gradients explaining up to 50% of the variance in the input data, rather than
focusing on the first one to three gradients as is often done in the literature.
Determining the unique contributions of factors with the potential to shift each gradient’s explained
variance (e.g., modality and its specific topographic properties, pre-processing, hyperparameters used to
generate the gradients) would require careful analysis and comparisons across a multitude of conditions.
However, we note that in the existing literature, the scaled eigenvalue as a measure of variance/information
explained of each gradient is usually computed on a smaller number of components. Previous work has
often restricted the number of computed gradients to a much lower number relative to the dimensionality
of their input data (parcellated with a higher resolution parcellation or using vertexwise data). In the present
case, we computed a relatively high number of gradients (99; restricted by the dimensionality of our
parcellated input data). For example, scaling the eigenvalues of the iEEG gradients according to the first
10 components increases the scaled eigenvalues of G1-G3 to 21.3%, 16.9%, and 14.2%. As a result, we
believe that the interaction between the dimensionality of the input data and the number of gradients
retained in the analysis affected the reported variance explained.
3.7 I assume that the 50% cutoff for selecting gradients was chosen because it's a nice big round number.
Do the results change meaningfully if only the first 3–5 gradients are used? I realise re-running all
analyses would be burdensome (though it could serve as a nice reproducibility check!). However, if you
can show that the correlation between the full embedding matrix (computed with G1–G14) and a reduced
matrix (e.g., computed with just G1–G2, G1–G3, etc.) remains high, that would suggest the results are
robust to the number of gradients included.
We found that the embedding distance matrix was highly correlated across many different combinations of
gradients from 2 to 14. The correlation matrix is shown below and has been added to our Supplementary
materials. We refer to this analysis in our revised RESULTS (p.6):
“This matrix was highly robust to the number of gradients included when calculating inter-nodes distances (FIGURE
S8)”
Figure S8. Robustness to variations in number of gradients included in embedding distance matrix. We
systematically varied the number of gradients included when computing inter-node embedding distances
and cross-correlated each matrix (excluding the diagonal). The resulting correlation matrix (min r = 0.902;
mean r = 0.965) shows high reproducibility of the embedding distance matrix when successively including
more gradients to compute embedding distances.
3.8 In Figure 2A, the matrix is labelled as indicating “Euclidean distance,” but in the following figure
it is described as “embedding distance.” While the embedding distance is indeed a Euclidean distance,
for consistency I suggest updating the colourbar label to “Embedding distance.” Also (as I am sure you
are aware) “Euclidean distance” is typically understood to refer to physical distances between parcels,
so to some people (i.e., me) labelling a matrix of the distances in high dimensional gradient space as
“Euclidean distance” may be confusing.
We thank Dr. Oldham for this helpful suggestion and updated the labelling in FIGURE 2A accordingly.
3.9 Also for Figure 2A: in the brain projection, could the seed parcel be made more visually prominent
or central? The selected hippocampal parcel is somewhat obscured, and I missed it at first glance.
We updated the figure following the Reviewer’s suggestion.
3.10 Is the geodesic distance measured in millimetres? The colour scale suggests a maximum distance
of 550 mm, which seems quite high. In my own data, the maximum geodesic distance across individuals
tends to be around 250–300 mm. Could you please double-check?
We use the Workbench Command function -surface-geodesic-distance to compute individual
geodesic distance matrices, which we believe to output distance in millimeters (although this does not seem
to be specified in the documentation). We speculate that the reason output distances are higher here might
be related to our use of high-resolution, native surfaces to compute the distances (coastline paradox).
In detail, we used micapipe (https://github.com/MICA-MNI/micapipe/) to align selected parcellations to the
native surface space, select a centroid vertex for each parcel, compute the geodesic distance of this centroid
vertex to all other surface vertices, and average distances within each parcel. We added this clarification to
the METHODS (p.18-19):
“Of note, longer distances measurements may be obtained here due to our use of high-resolution meshes, compared
to techniques using surfaces resampled according to a lower-resolution template’s geometry.”
3.11 For Figure 3B, it wasn’t immediately clear that the colours of the bars correspond to the colours of
the matrices for each feature. I think there’s enough space in the legend to explicitly state what each
colour represents.
This information was added to the revised legend (p.10):
“The colour of the bars corresponds to the different MRI modalities shown in panel A (blue: GD; orange: SC; pink:
FC; green: MPC).”
3.12 Also for Figure 3B: are the ridge plots showing the distribution of bootstrap results? This isn’t
stated clearly. Is the vertical line the mean or median of the bootstrap distribution, and is the dot the non-
bootstrapped result?
This is indeed correct, and the information was added to the revised legend (p.10):
“Each ridge plot shows the distribution of bootstrap results, with their median value indicated by the black line. The
black dot marker indicates the true adjusted r2 for each model.”
3.13 For Figure 3C: in the far-right plot showing correlations with FC G1, is the variable shown the
correlation between nodal FC G1 values and the full model–baseline difference from the previous plot?
If so, could you ensure the name of this variable is consistent across figures to help with interpretation?
This specific correlation (full model – baseline model difference) corresponds to the rightmost marker in
this plot (dark red). The other markers show the correlations values for each combination of partial model
– baseline model difference. We have changed the label of the y-axis to better reflect this.
3.14 Figure 4A: what does the rainbow line overlaid on the brain slices represent?
We added this information to the revised caption of FIGURE 4 (p.12):
“The coloured markers overlaid on the T1-weighted images indicate the locations of contacts of a single electrode
implanted in this patient (deeper contacts in blue, superficial contacts in orange).”
3.15 The paragraphs in the Discussion section are quite long. Breaking them up would improve
readability.
We followed the Reviewer’s suggestion and have broken up the paragraphs of the DISCUSSION.
3.16 (Remarks on code availability): I quickly checked the code, seems to all run and reproduce the
results in the paper.
We thank the Reviewer for verifying the replication scripts provided in the repository.

review_generation.input:
You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The brain is a physically embedded and heavily interconnected system that expresses neural rhythms across multiple timescales. While these dynamics result from the complex interplay of local and inter-regional factors, the relative contribution of such mechanisms across the cortex remains unclear. Our study explores geometric, microstructural, and connectome-level constraints on cortex-wide neural activity. We leverage intracranial electroencephalography recordings to derive a coordinate system of human cortical dynamics. Using multimodal neuroimaging, we could then demonstrate that these patterns are largely explainable by geometric properties indexed by inter-regional distance. However, dynamics in transmodal association regions are additionally explainable by incorporation of inter-regional microstructural similarity and connectivity information. Our findings are generally consistent when cross-referencing electroencephalography and imaging data from large-scale atlases and when using data obtained in the same individuals, suggesting subject-specificity and population-level generalizability. Together, our results suggest that the relative contribution of local and macroscale constraints on cortical dynamics varies systematically across the cortical sheet, specifically highlighting the role of transmodal networks in inter-regional cortical coordination.

---

## Introduction

The brain generates nested and propagating rhythms from the synchronized firing of neuronal ensembles1. These dynamics signals are a core feature of brain organization, serving as established markers of brain health2–4, neural communication5–7, vigilance, and cognitive states8–15. Intracranial electroencephalography (iEEG) offers a unique window into these rhythms. Moving beyond spatially restricted recordings performed in individual patients16,17 recent data sharing initiatives have provided comprehensive maps of human neurophysiology and unlocked new avenues to study inter-regional heterogeneity in neural dynamics8,18. However, technical challenges relating to multimodal data availability, registration, and integration across and within patient cohorts have particularly hindered these investigations, which have so far been limited to single scales of inquiry. The present work fills this gap by uncovering large-scale gradients of neural dynamics and relating this complex activity landscape to underlying multiscale anatomy.

Prior work has demonstrated distinct neurophysiological signatures operating across distributed cortical territories19. These signatures generally follow overlapping spatial gradients of cortical microarchitecture involving neurotransmitter receptors and transporters, gene expression, metabolic demands, cortical thickness, and proxies of intracortical myelination20–22. Relatedly, focal lesions altering local anatomy and microarchitecture co-localize with atypical neural dynamics2,3. While this evidence supports the role of intrinsic physiological mechanisms in generating regional neural activity23,24, local structural features can only partially explain spatial variations in neural dynamics. For instance, areas made up of fundamentally different milieus can also produce rhythms with similar features: peaks in beta-range activity have been recorded in large parts of the frontal lobe, from the precentral gyrus to the frontal pole, as well as portions of the parietal lobe and the anterior insula18. As such, network-level propagation of brain activity via direct structural connections as well as polysynaptic functional interactions has also been suggested to account for this inter-regional variability25. Indeed, local dynamics systematically vary along the cortical processing hierarchy, as demonstrated by task paradigms, stimulation work, and in silico explorations26–28. Resting dynamics also propagate to nearby regions via traveling waves, scaffolded by the brain’s short- and long-range connections29, producing a complex mosaic of intrinsic and extrinsic constraints on neural dynamics.

Such multiscale inquiries can be achieved by integrating the high spatiotemporal precision of iEEG with recent methodological and analytical advances in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) offering complementary insights into cortico-cortical network organization. At the most basic level is cortical geometry, which reflects the proximity of brain regions. The brain is a physically embedded network, with adjacent regions generally participating in similar functional processes30. Moreover, adjacent regions are generally strongly connected via intracortical axon collaterals and superficial white matter fibers31, which closely regulate local neural activity32,33. A further important component of brain network architecture is local intracortical microstructure, which has classically been studied using cytoarchitectonic mapping of post-mortem tissue34. Recently, similar approaches have been translated to in vivo MRI using myelin-sensitive contrasts, such as T1 relaxometry35–38. Both lines of investigation suggest that regions with similar microstructure generally participate in corresponding functional processes and are more likely to share a direct structural connection34,35,39,40. Beyond the study of local geometry and microstructure, techniques such as diffusion MRI tractography and functional MRI connectivity have characterized large-scale, regionally distributed structural and functional networks. While the former approximates long-range, white matter fiber tracts in vivo41–44, the latter taps into spatially distributed, and often polysynaptic intrinsic networks45–47. In line with recently developed composite wiring diagrams of the human cortex emphasizing a synergy of different MRI modalities in predicting macroscale function48–54, simultaneous consideration of these diverse modalities elucidates the contribution of short- and long-range network information to human cortical dynamics.

Our goal was (i) to chart the cortical topography of neural rhythms in the human brain interrogated with iEEG18, and (ii) identify the differential association between cortical dynamics and network organization mapped with multimodal MRI55. Applying dimensionality reduction to a cortex-wide assessment of inter-regional iEEG power spectra similarity allowed us to situate cortical areas within a compact embedding space constrained by their dynamics. These gradients, mapped here in iEEG data, captured the coordinate system of neural rhythms in the neocortex, grouping regions with similar neurophysiology independently of their anatomic allocation. We then quantified the contribution of different network level features to the topography of neural dynamics using multilinear spatial statistics at a cortex-wide scale. We complemented this approach with region-specific models capturing the relative contribution of each network metric across cortical areas, and tracked how these contributions varied along the cortical processing hierarchy56. Our assessment was based on independent datasets and systematic variations of analysis parameters to identify robust associations between human cortical dynamics and multiscale network features.

## Results

Mapping cortical gradients of neural dynamics
For the main analyses, we leveraged a Discovery cohort (MNI open iEEG atlas, n=106) in which iEEG data were aggregated in stereotactic space18. We assessed correspondence to neural organization derived from two high-definition MRI datasets acquired in 50 healthy individuals at 3T and 10 healthy individuals at 7T. Our main analyses thus rest on a design comparing iEEG and imaging modalities across two different datasets. We then evaluate the generalizability of our findings using a fully independent Replication cohort (MNI clinical dataset, n=18), where both iEEG and multimodal pre-surgical MRI data were available in each participant for within-cohort comparison of modalities.

The MNI open iEEG atlas includes recordings from 106 patients with intractable epilepsy, totaling over 1700 data points taken from non-epileptic channels registered to the MNI152 reference space18. Mapping all channels to a single hemisphere as in previous work8,18 granted wide sampling of the cortical sheet (Fig. 1A). Spatial heterogeneity of spectral features was visible across channels, but could also be recovered when averaging channel power spectra within larger cortical regions (Fig. 1B)57. We captured spatial variations in macroscale neural dynamics by applying dimensionality reduction to similarity patterns in regional power spectra (Fig. 1C). After averaging vertex-wise, log-transformed power spectral densities (PSDs) within parcels, regional PSDs were cross-correlated while accounting for the cortex-wide average power spectrum using partial correlations. We converted the result to a normalized angle affinity matrix and applied diffusion map embedding, a nonlinear dimensionality reduction technique, to recover eigenvectors (gradients) of macroscale similarity in regional neural dynamics. We retained gradients explaining a cumulative sum of 50% of the variance for further analyses (G1–G14; see Fig. S1A for the topography of these gradients). The embedding space formed by the first two gradients (explaining 17.37% of the variance in PSD similarity) was used as a complementary visualization of findings.

The first gradient (G1) evolved along the anterior-posterior direction, mainly differentiating primary motor and surrounding lateral prefrontal cortices from unimodal sensory regions (Fig. 1D). G1 indeed mainly followed the structural stratification defined by Von Economo and Koskinas58–60. This suggests a close correspondence between the axis of neurophysiological differentiation captured by G1 and regional heterogeneity in laminar differentiation, notably segregating “input” sensory regions with a granular structure from “output” motor areas with an agranular structure (Fig. S1B). This gradient mirrored regional variations in spectral peaks by segregating areas with strong beta and gamma-range activity from areas showing prominent delta, theta, and alpha-range peaks18. Next, G2 differentiated unimodal sensorimotor from transmodal cortices, recapitulating the previously established principal axis of cortical connectivity and functional hierarchy (Fig. 1D)61. Indeed, G2 was specifically correlated with the unimodal-transmodal gradient of cortical organization derived from functional MRI (Spearman r=0.564; p < 0.001; Fig. S1C; correlations with all other gradients did not survive Bonferroni correction). This pattern segregated regions showing predominant lower frequency activity from other cortical areas with peaks occurring above the delta frequency range. The two-dimensional representation of neural dynamics formed by these gradients separated unimodal sensory regions, precentral motor areas, and spatially distributed transmodal systems (Fig. 1E). Cortical surface plots shown in Fig. 1B furthermore highlighted consistency of regional power spectra amplitudes with previously published normative maps of neocortical dynamics2,3,62. We observed higher delta band power in frontal, parietal, and temporal cortices relative to unimodal sensory and motor regions. High alpha- and beta-range power was observed within occipital and precentral regions, respectively, while a rostro-caudal shift was observed in gamma-range activity across the cortex. Collectively, these results map gradients of neural rhythms able to resolve fine-grained oscillatory activity of individual channels. We additionally show that these gradient recover macroscale trends in the overall similarity of spectral content across the cortex.

Control analyses were implemented to assess the robustness of described gradients and embedding space. First, results were robust to the use of different parcellation schemes (Fig. S2). Indeed, generating gradients from unparcellated PSD data (i.e., channel regions—see “Materials and methods”) or averaging PSDs within nodes defined by two different atlases (i.e., Glasser-360 and a subdivision of the aparc parcellation) yielded similar topographies for both G1 (vertexwise Spearman correlations for unparcellated: r=0.673; Glasser-360: r=0.839; aparc-200 r=0.864) and G2 (vertexwise Spearman correlations for unparcellated: r=0.524; Glasser-360: r=0.580; aparc-200 r=0.645). Furthermore, we could recover the topography of the first 10 gradients when imposing an upper bound to the number of channels included in each parcel of the Schaefer-200 parcellation (Fig. S3), suggesting that our findings could not be attributed to variable channel coverage across nodes. We also replicated our findings when preserving the bilateral distribution of channels and applying a lower resolution parcellation (Schaefer-100) to maintain broad cortical coverage (Fig. S4). The high correspondence of G1 (vertexwise Spearman correlation r_left=0.767; r_right=0.804) and G2 (vertexwise Spearman correlation r_left=0.645; r_right=0.671) topographies with gradients derived from our main analysis provides additional support for the independence of our findings to parcellation choice. Lastly, spatial correlations assessing the consistency of gradients across a range of hyperparameter combinations were generally very strong (Fig. S7).

Multiscale connectomics of neural dynamics
After establishing the topography of macroscale gradients of neural dynamics, we investigated how this embedding space co-varied with multiscale properties of brain network organization. All network measures were gathered from an independent cohort of 50 unrelated, healthy volunteers that underwent multimodal 3T MRI (23 women; age mean ± standard deviation = 30.28 ± 5.74 years)55. We first computed the Euclidean distance between all node pairs in the embedding space, which served as a proxy for inter-node similarity in neural dynamics (embedding distance, Fig. 2A). This matrix was highly robust to the number of gradients included when calculating inter-node distances (Fig. S8). Node proximity in the embedding space was cross-referenced with measures of (i) cortical geometry indexed by inter-node geodesic distance computed along the surface mesh (geodesic distance, GD), (ii) tractography-based structural connectivity (SC), (iii) intrinsic functional connectivity generated from resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), and (iv) microstructural profile covariance (MPC) derived from T1 relaxometry. Matrices were computed for each participant and averaged across individuals (for details on data processing, analysis, and group-level aggregation, see “Materials and methods”). Multimodal associations were computed by correlating the upper triangular edges of each matrix. We only considered MRI data from the right hemisphere, as all iEEG data had been transposed to the right hemisphere to improve cortical coverage. For each modality, statistical significance was determined by comparing empirically observed correlations to those obtained with surrogate matrices in which each row had been shuffled using spatial autocorrelation-preserving null models63,64.

We first observed a moderate correlation (r=-0.376; p < 0.001) between GD of cortical regions and embedding distance, indicating that nodes with similar dynamics were situated closer to each other along the cortical sheet (Fig. 2B). Node-wise correlations between both modalities were particularly strong in anterior and posterior lateral regions. We also obtained a moderate correlation (r=-0.341; p < 0.001) between edge strength of the SC matrix and embedding distance, suggesting closer neural dynamic similarity between regions sharing stronger structural connections (Fig. 2C). Regional SC and embedding distances were most strongly correlated in lateral frontal and temporal regions. Polysynaptic network architectures captured by the functional connectome were weakly, yet significantly, correlated with embedding distances (r=-0.227; p < 0.001), once again indicating stronger connections between regions sharing similar neural dynamics (Fig. 2D). This relationship was particularly strong in medial and lateral prefrontal, as well as medial occipito-temporal regions. Lastly, embedding distance was significantly yet more weakly correlated with MPC (r=-0.170; p < 0.001), with significant correlations confined to heteromodal and paralimbic cortical structures such as mesial temporal and frontal regions, as well as the precuneus and lateral parietal areas (Fig. 2E). Of note, relationships between neocortical dynamics similarity and multiscale connectivity measures were consistent when binarizing network matrices across a wide range of thresholds (Fig. 2B–E). Findings were replicable when cross-referencing embedding distances with multimodal data collected in a distinct set of participants scanned at 7T MRI65 (Fig. S5), and when computing correlations between embedding distances and MRI measures from bilaterally mapped data (SC r=-0.322; FC r=-0.217; MPC r=-0.185). Together, these results demonstrate that neural dynamics similarity is most strongly associated with cortical geometry indexed by geodesic distance, with weaker yet statistically significant relationships to large-scale network metrics. Modality-specific correlations were nonetheless highly variable across regions.

These results show regional variations in the relative contributions of different network properties to cortical dynamics, while emphasizing the stronger relationship with spatial proximity between nodes. We next sought to clarify the combined contribution of network features to neural dynamic similarity by quantifying potential gains in model accuracy when considering multiscale network properties over GD alone. To do so, we constructed several multiple linear regression models, in which we varied the combination of predictors implemented in the model as well as the nature of the predicted and predictor variables. A baseline model including GD as its only predictor was used to benchmark the performance of the more complex models incorporating multimodal predictor sets. These models encompassed partial models with two (GD and another modality) or three predictors (GD and two other modalities) in addition to a full model with four predictors (all modalities; Fig. 3A).

Constructing this model across all unique edges (i.e., the upper triangle of each matrix) highlighted the strong contribution of GD relative to other modalities across all models (Fig. 3B). Notably, more complex models provided minimal gains in prediction accuracy, either when implementing the model on all data points (range of adjusted r^2 = 0.147–0.171) or when bootstrapping the data (90% train and 10% test; 1000 permutations; range of median adjusted r^2 = 0.142–0.161). We assessed cross-model accuracy variations by correlating the prediction error for each edge with the number of predictors in the corresponding model. In this approach, negative correlations indicate decreasing error with more complex models (i.e., high prediction accuracy for models with more predictors), while positive correlations indicate increasing error with more complex models (i.e., including additional predictors resulted in a noisier model). Our results show overall accuracy gains with increasing model complexity in mesial and anterolateral temporal, orbitofrontal, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortices, as well as the precuneus, while opposite trends were observed primarily in occipito-parietal regions (Fig. 3B, right). These findings indicate heterogeneous contributions of network predictors across cortical regions.

We further explored region-specific associations between multiscale network features to neural dynamic similarity by fitting distinct multiple linear regression models for each node’s connections and comparing model accuracy across different predictor combinations (Fig. 3C). For instance, when comparing baseline (GD only) and full (all network features) models, the greatest gains in adjusted r^2 were seen in dorsal lateral and medial frontal cortices, orbitofrontal, mesiotemporal, lateral parietal and precuneus regions. Regional differences in accuracy gains across certain model pairs were significantly correlated with the cortical processing hierarchy represented by the principal gradient of intrinsic functional connectivity56,66. More specifically, regional gains in model accuracy were significantly correlated with this gradient in models including both GD and MPC as predictors over GD alone, and accuracy could be further increased by including either SC or FC. These findings were replicated using an alternate representation of this hierarchy mapping four functional zones co-localizing with regional changes in cortical laminar elaboration61,67 (Fig. S6). These findings suggest a complementarity of local geometry and microstructure in supporting macroscale similarity of neural dynamics.

Replicability of gradients of neural dynamics
Our work mapped the landscape of neural dynamics similarity of the cortex and decoded its multiscale network correlates using multilinear spatial statistics. We lastly leveraged an independent patient cohort to assess the replicability of macroscale gradients of neural dynamics and their association with within-sample neuroimaging metrics. The MNI clinical dataset (Replication cohort) includes 18 patients who underwent high-resolution multimodal MRI prior to clinical iEEG investigations, allowing for precise, patient-specific segmentation of cortical gray matter, co-registration of iEEG contacts, and cross-referencing to within-sample connectivity measurements. Although all data modalities were available in patients of the Replication cohort, these replication analyses study a completely distinct sample of participants relative to the Discovery cohort, for both iEEG and MRI metrics.

Following the same analytical pipeline as in our main analysis, electrophysiological data from all patients was combined to generate group-level gradients of neural dynamic similarity (Fig. 4A). The gradient space in this independent sample segregated temporo-parietal regions and frontal cortices along G1, and distinguished transmodal temporal and frontal structures from lower-order sensorimotor areas along G2 (Fig. 4B). The first 13 gradients, explaining a cumulative 50% of the variance in the input data, were all significantly correlated (p < 0.05; p < 0.003 with Bonferroni correction) with their corresponding gradient in the Discovery sample (after Procrustes alignment including translation, rotation, and scaling: mean ± SD Spearman r = 0.509 ± 0.076). After alignment, we found a significant correlation between the embedding distance matrices of Discovery and Replication cohorts (r = 0.304; p < 0.001), with variable similarity across regions (Fig. S9). We also applied a more conservative alignment strategy where Replication cohort gradients were reordered to optimally match (i.e., minimize the distance) with the Discovery cohort eigenvectors. With this approach, correlations were overall lower but also indicated generalizability of main findings in the Replication cohort (mean ± SD Spearman r = 0.196 ± 0.154; Fig. S10). Systematic within-cohort and cross-cohort correlations spanning the gradient hyperparameter space found the resulting gradients to be generally robust to parameter selection (Fig. S7). Differences in vertex-wise channel coverage between both cohorts partly contributed to node-wise displacement in the embedding space (Fig. 4B). Channel coverage in the Replication cohort was notably higher in lateral temporal regions, and lower in insular and frontal cortices. The coverage difference map across datasets was significantly correlated with average node rank changes between each gradient (r = -0.179; p = 0.038), suggesting that regional differences in channel coverage across the datasets may partially account for node shifts in the resulting embedding space.

Bivariate associations between each MRI modality and embedding distances specific to the Replication cohort again highlighted strongest correlations with GD (r = -0.323; p = 0.002), and relatively balanced correlations with SC (r = -0.233; p < 0.001), FC (r = -0.264; p < 0.001), and MPC (r = -0.256; p < 0.001) (Fig. 4C). This stronger contribution of GD was replicated in all multilinear models. The contribution of SC in these models was negligible when either FC or MPC was included as a model predictor. Of all modalities, SC was the most dissimilar across cohorts (cross-cohort correlations for each matrix: r_GD = 0.999; r_SC = 0.847; r_FC = 0.960; r_MPC = 0.947). Bivariate correlations between Replication cohort embedding distance and connectome matrices computed from our sample of healthy participants (as used in our Discovery cohort analysis) recovered the overall pattern of findings observed in the Discovery cohort, with descending correlation strength with GD (r = -0.323), SC (r = -0.268), FC (r = -0.250), and MPC (r = -0.245). These findings indicate modality-specific idiosyncrasies potentially sensitive to epilepsy-related connectome alterations when comparing findings across datasets. Leveraging within-sample data furthermore highlighted overall improved prediction of neural dynamics similarity over all edges with increasing model complexity, particularly when including FC and MPC as model predictors (Fig. 4C). When using iEEG and connectivity data extracted from distinct samples (as done in our Discovery cohort analysis), this effect was only observed in transmodal cortices and when selectively fitting models at the node-level. In additional replication analyses implemented at the individual level, we also found stronger associations with GD relative to other modalities, followed by SC and balanced correlations with FC and MPC (Fig. S11). Furthermore, reconstructing the embedding space while iteratively excluding each patient showed that embedding distances between nodes related to channel-specific PSD similarity in the held-out patient (Fig. S12). Together, these findings demonstrate the overall replicability of our main findings across cohorts as well as within-patient generalizability, while additionally identifying nuances in long-range wiring principles of neural dynamics in different analytical designs (between- versus within-subject).
